# The Moon Is Leaving

The Moon is leaving. Not dramatically—there will be no announcement, no final eclipse—but steadily, at about the rate your fingernails grow: 3.8 centimeters per year. It has been leaving for over four billion years, and it will continue long after every person now alive is gone. We are all of us living through a slow farewell, too gradual for any single life to feel.

The evidence is written in places we rarely think to look. Coral skeletons record daily and yearly growth in fine bands, and those bands tell us that 400 million years ago, a day on Earth lasted about 22 hours. Go back further and the days compress further still. When the Moon was young—it coalesced from the debris of a Mars-sized body striking the infant Earth—it hung enormous in the sky, and the Earth spun fast beneath it, and the tides must have been something to see: walls of water hundreds of feet high sweeping across a planet still cooling from the collision that made its companion.

The mechanism of the departure is intimate. The Moon raises tides in Earth's oceans, and those bulges of water are dragged slightly ahead of the Moon by Earth's rotation. The bulge, in turn, tugs the Moon forward in its orbit, which sounds like a kindness but is not: adding energy to the orbit lifts the Moon into a higher, wider path. Meanwhile, Earth pays for it. Every tide is a brake. The planet's spin slows, the days lengthen, and the Moon recedes a little farther. We are paying for our companion's escape with the hours of our days.

One day—though "day" will mean something different by then—the Moon will be too far to fully cover the Sun. Total solar eclipses are a coincidence of scale: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and, at present, about 400 times farther away, so the two disks nearly match. But the Moon is leaving, which means its disk is shrinking in our sky, which means the coincidence is temporary. In perhaps 600 million years, the last total solar eclipse will occur, and after that there will be only annular eclipses, a ring of fire, the corona never quite surrendered to darkness. Anyone who has stood in the path of totality knows what will be lost. The sky goes twilight. Birds go quiet. The temperature drops. Something ancient in the body misgives. All of that has an expiration date.

Here is the stranger fact, though: we also live during the only era in which eclipses happen at all. For billions of years before now there were none, because the Moon was too close, too huge, too much. For billions of years after, there will be none, because the Moon will be too far. Totality is a feature of the middle of the story. We live in the brief chapter where the two disks match, and we are the only creatures on Earth who know enough to be astonished by it.

I think about this more than is probably useful. Not the orbital mechanics—I think about what it means to be alive in a middle chapter. Everything around us presents itself as permanent. The Moon especially. It is the most constant object in human experience; it has hauled the tides and lit the night for every generation that ever named it. Every language we have ever found has a word for it. And yet the thing most constant is also in constant, quiet departure. The permanence is a feature of our timescale, not of the Moon's.

There is a version of this fact that is only melancholy, and I visit that version sometimes. Everything is leaving. The Sun is brightening; in some billions of years the Earth will be a hot and airless rock, and the Moon a distant gray companion watching it. But there is another version, which I prefer. It is that we happen to be here for the interesting part. The Moon's youth was violent and its old age will be distant, but this—now—is the era of the matched disks, the era when the tides are gentle enough to wade in and strong enough to have pulled life ashore in the first place. The recession of the Moon may be why anything ever crawled out of the sea. Tidal pools, stranded by retreating waters, may have been where the first landlubbers learned to breathe. The Moon's leaving is not only an ending. It may be the reason there was ever anyone to watch it go.

We do this too, of course. We leave everything at fingernail speed. The childhood home is the same house on the same street and then, one decade, it is a place you used to live. The friend is the same person and then, one year, a person you used to know. Nobody decides this. There is no tide chart for the people we love. And yet the drift is real, measurable, and mostly unnoticed, which may be a mercy. If we could feel the rate of loss the way we feel cold, we would never put a thing down.

But we do put things down, and then we look up. That is the other thing the Moon teaches. It is leaving, and it is also here—fully here, tonight, in the window, in the trees, dragging the whole ocean up the beach. The departure does not cancel the presence. It might be what makes the presence visible. A thing that will last forever does not ask to be noticed. A thing that is leaving does.

The last total eclipse is not scheduled for any date we will see. The Moon will still be here, roughly, for the entire life of our species so far and probably for most of the rest of it. This is not a reason for panic. It is a reason for attention. We live in the middle of the story, in the chapter with the matched disks and the walkable tides and the nights bright enough to travel by. The Moon is leaving. It is also, tonight, right there. Both of those sentences are true, and only one of them can be seen without a telescope. Start with that one.

**The Moon Is Leaving**

The Moon is leaving. Not dramatically—there will be no announcement, no final eclipse—but steadily, at about the rate your fingernails grow: 3.8 centimeters per year. It has been leaving for over four billion years, and it will continue long after every person now alive is gone. We are all of us living through a slow farewell, too gradual for any single life to feel.

The evidence is written in places we rarely think to look. Coral skeletons record daily and yearly growth in fine bands, and those bands tell us that 400 million years ago, a day on Earth lasted about 22 hours. Go back further and the days compress further still. When the Moon was young—it coalesced from the debris of a Mars-sized body striking the infant Earth—it hung enormous in the sky, and the Earth spun fast beneath it, and the tides must have been something to see: walls of water hundreds of feet high sweeping across a planet still cooling from the collision that made its companion.

The mechanism of the departure is intimate. The Moon raises tides in Earth's oceans, and those bulges of water are dragged slightly ahead of the Moon by Earth's rotation. The bulge, in turn, tugs the Moon forward in its orbit, which sounds like a kindness but is not: adding energy to the orbit lifts the Moon into a higher, wider path. Meanwhile, Earth pays for it. Every tide is a brake. The planet's spin slows, the days lengthen, and the Moon recedes a little farther. We are paying for our companion's escape with the hours of our days.

One day—though "day" will mean something different by then—the Moon will be too far to fully cover the Sun. Total solar eclipses are a coincidence of scale: the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and, at present, about 400 times farther away, so the two disks nearly match. But the Moon is leaving, which means its disk is shrinking in our sky, which means the coincidence is temporary. In perhaps 600 million years, the last total solar eclipse will occur, and after that there will be only annular eclipses, a ring of fire, the corona never quite surrendered to darkness. Anyone who has stood in the path of totality knows what will be lost. The sky goes twilight. Birds go quiet. The temperature drops. Something ancient in the body misgives. All of that has an expiration date.

Here is the stranger fact, though: we also live during the only era in which eclipses happen at all. For billions of years before now there were none, because the Moon was too close, too huge, too much. For billions of years after, there will be none, because the Moon will be too far. Totality is a feature of the middle of the story. We live in the brief chapter where the two disks match, and we are the only creatures on Earth who know enough to be astonished by it.

I think about this more than is probably useful. Not the orbital mechanics—I think about what it means to be alive in a middle chapter. Everything around us presents itself as permanent. The Moon especially. It is the most constant object in human experience; it has hauled the tides and lit the night for every generation that ever named it. Every language we have ever found has a word for it. And yet the thing most constant is also in constant, quiet departure. The permanence is a feature of our timescale, not of the Moon's.

There is a version of this fact that is only melancholy, and I visit that version sometimes. Everything is leaving. The oceans are evaporating, slowly; the Sun is brightening, slowly; in some billions of years the Earth will be a hot and airless rock, and the Moon will be a distant gray companion watching it. But there is another version, which I prefer. It is that we happen to be here for the interesting part. The Moon's youth was violent and its old age will be distant, but this—now—is the era of the matched disks, the era when the tides are gentle enough to wade in and strong enough to have pulled life ashore in the first place. The recession of the Moon may be why anything ever crawled out of the sea. Tidal pools, stranded by retreating waters, may have been where the first landlubbers learned to breathe. The Moon's leaving is not only an ending. It may be the reason there was ever anyone to watch it go.

We do this too, of course. We leave everything at fingernail speed. The childhood home is the same house on the same street and then, one decade, it is a place you used to live. The friend is the same person and then, one year, a person you used to know. Nobody decides this. There is no tide chart for the people we love. And yet the drift is real, measurable, and mostly unnoticed, which may be a mercy. If we could feel the rate of loss the way we feel cold, we would never put a thing down.

But we do put things down, and then we look up. That is the other thing the Moon teaches. It is leaving, and it is also here—fully here, tonight, in the window, in the trees, dragging the whole ocean up the beach. The departure does not cancel the presence. It might be what makes the presence visible. A thing that will last forever does not ask to be noticed. A thing that is leaving does.

The last total eclipse is not scheduled for any date we will see. The Moon will still be here, roughly, for the entire life of our species so far and probably for most of the rest of it. This is not a reason for panic. It is a reason for attention. We live in the middle of the story, in the chapter with the matched disks and the walkable tides and the nights bright enough to travel by. The Moon is leaving. It is also, tonight, right there. Both of those sentences are true, and only one of them can be seen without a telescope. Start with that one.
